newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast says donors must accept slower reforms.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast says donors must accept slower reforms.

text.p: Ivory Coast favours total liberalisation of cocoa and coffee marketing but says donors must accept gradual implementation.

"We say to the World Bank that we are for total liberalisation but on condition that we get there at our own pace," Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan said in an interview with the Paris-based weekly magazine Jeune Afrique.
Privatisation of the Caistab commodities board would also be considered, he said in the interview published ahead of talks next week with donors.
"Privatise the Caistab? Why not. There is no taboo," he said, adding that help would be given to farmers' cooperatives, which have no legal foundation, to set up as private businesses.
"I will present shortly a new bill aimed at better organisation and more responsibility for cooperatives," he said, adding that professional agricultural bodies also needed help.
Ivory Coast has loosened its monopoly on cocoa and coffee marketing since 1995 under terms for a $150 million agriculture credit from the World Bank -- which wants further changes.
Cocoa and coffee liberalisation are on a wider agenda for donor talks next week on a three-year economic plan for Ivory Coast and its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.
Donors want the state Caistab commodities board to hand farm-to-port price-setting to the private sector, with exporters possibly assuming a greater role in export auction management.
Ivory Coast has agreed to sweeping coffee marketing reforms from 1998/99, and more limited measures by 1999/2000 for cocoa.
Details have yet to be finalised and officially announced.
Ivory Coast supplies up to 40 percent of the world's cocoa and is the world's largest producer. It is also Africa's main robusta coffee producer.

Ivory Coast has around three million planters, with farms averaging 2.5 hectares. Exporters in 1995/96 took over responsibility for transport and jute sack distribution to farmers -- who complain exporters have pocketed allowances and forced them to buy their own.
"It is more proof that total liberalisition is not a panacea," Kouassi said.
Donors want farm prices raised for 1997/98. Kouassi said the reference coffee price was likely to rise from 500 CFA francs.
He said high world coffee prices had profited the Caistab although revisions of commodity auctions pricing rules would be adopted after complaints of overbidding for export contracts.
"The auction has on the whole been satisfactory," said Kouassi. Ivory Coast had agreed with donors to allow three highest bidding exporters to win at the price they bid, he said.
Current rules award contracts to the highest bidder, but at the second highest bid price offered in the trading session.
